e-5904.worked_solution:
First, we find the matrix $\, A-\lambda I \mathbin{:}$

﻿﻿﻿![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14069899/assets/8bfd617b360f6bed1fcf835ebe52c56f3c7b6a5a5234e099f7a0aec0d4bbdc36.png)

Then, we compute the characteristic equation, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A-\lambda I) & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}1-\lambda  & -2 \\ 2 & 1-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (1-\lambda )(1-\lambda )-2(-2) & =0 \\ 1-2\lambda +{\lambda }^{2}+4 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-2\lambda +5 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Using the quadratic formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\lambda  & =\frac{-b\pm \sqrt{{b}^{2}-4ac}}{2a} \\  & =\frac{-(-2)\pm \sqrt{(-2)^{2}-4(1)(5)}}{2(1)} \\  & =\frac{2\pm \sqrt{-16}}{2} \\  & =\frac{2\pm 4\text{i}}{2} \\  & =1\pm 2\text{i}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the eigenvalues are $\lambda=1\pm 2\textrm{i}.$

e-5905.knowledge_point: Finding a Complex Eigenvalue of a 2x2 Matrix Given Another Eigenvalue
e-5905.problem: Given that $\lambda_1=-2+3\textrm{i}$ and $\lambda_2$ are eigenvalues of a real $2 \times 2$ matrix $A,$ find $2(\lambda_1+\lambda_2).$
e-5905.worked_solution:
Since $\lambda_1=-2+3\textrm{i}$ is a complex eigenvalue of $A,$ the second eigenvalue of $A$ must be the complex conjugate of $\lambda_1.$
Therefore, 

$$
\lambda_2=\overline{\lambda}_1=-2-3\textrm{i}.
$$

Finally, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}2({\lambda }_{1}+{\lambda }_{2}) & =2(-2+3\text{i}+(-2-3\text{i})) \\  & =2(-4) \\  & =-8.\end{aligned}
$$

after.name: Question 2
after.problem: Compute the eigenvalues of the matrix $A=[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ 4 & 5\end{aligned}].$
after.worked_solution:
First, we find the matrix $\,A-\lambda I:$
﻿﻿﻿

$$
A-\lambda I=[\begin{aligned}1-\lambda  & -2 \\ 4 & 5-\lambda \end{aligned}]
$$

Then, we compute the characteristic equation, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A-\lambda I) & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}1-\lambda  & -2 \\ 4 & 5-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (1-\lambda )(5-\lambda )-4(-2) & =0 \\ 5-\lambda -5\lambda +{\lambda }^{2}+8 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-6\lambda +13 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Using the quadratic formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\lambda  & =\frac{-b\pm \sqrt{{b}^{2}-4ac}}{2a} \\  & =\frac{6\pm \sqrt{(-6)^{2}-4(1)(13)}}{2(1)} \\  & =\frac{6\pm \sqrt{-16}}{2} \\  & =\frac{6\pm 4\text{i}}{2} \\  & =3\pm 2\text{i}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the eigenvalues are $\lambda =3\pm 2\text{i}.$

content.problem: Compute the eigenvalues of the matrix $A=[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 3 & 1\end{aligned}].$

First, we find the matrix $\,A-\lambda I:$
﻿﻿﻿

$$
A-\lambda I=[\begin{aligned}1-\lambda  & -1 \\ 3 & 1-\lambda \end{aligned}]
$$

Then, we compute the characteristic equation, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A-\lambda I) & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}1-\lambda  & -1 \\ 3 & 1-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (1-\lambda )(1-\lambda )-(-1)(3) & =0 \\ 1-2\lambda +{\lambda }^{2}+3 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-2\lambda +4 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Using the quadratic formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\lambda  & =\frac{-b\pm \sqrt{{b}^{2}-4ac}}{2a} \\  & =\frac{-(-2)\pm \sqrt{(-2)^{2}-4(1)(4)}}{2(1)} \\  & =\frac{2\pm \sqrt{-12}}{2} \\  & =\frac{2\pm 2\sqrt{3}\text{i}}{2} \\  & =1\pm \sqrt{3}\text{i}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the eigenvalues are $\lambda =1\pm \sqrt{3}\text{i}.$

after.name: Question 5
after.problem: Compute the eigenvalues of the matrix $A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ -2 & -1\end{aligned}].$
after.worked_solution:
First, we find the matrix $\,A-\lambda I:$
﻿﻿﻿

$$
A-\lambda I=[\begin{aligned}1-\lambda  & 1 \\ -2 & -1-\lambda \end{aligned}]
$$

Then, we compute the characteristic equation, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A-\lambda I) & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}1-\lambda  & 1 \\ -2 & -1-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (1-\lambda )(-1-\lambda )-1(-2) & =0 \\ -1-\lambda +\lambda +{\lambda }^{2}+2 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}+1 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2} & =-1 \\ \lambda  & =\pm \text{i}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the eigenvalues are $\lambda =\pm \text{i}.$

after.name: Question 6
after.problem: Given that ${\lambda }_{1}=-5+4\text{i}$ and ${\lambda }_{2}$ are eigenvalues of a real $2\times 2$ matrix $A$, find $\frac{2}{5}({\lambda }_{1}+{\lambda }_{2}).$
after.worked_solution:
Since ${\lambda }_{1}=-5+4\text{i}$ is a complex eigenvalue of $A,$ the second eigenvalue of $A$ must be the complex conjugate of ${\lambda }_{1}.$
Therefore, 

$$
{\lambda }_{2}={\overset{―}{\lambda }}_{1}=-5-4\text{i}.
$$

Finally, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{5}({\lambda }_{1}+{\lambda }_{2}) & =\frac{2}{5}((-5+4\text{i})+(-5-4\text{i})) \\  & =\frac{2}{5}(-10) \\  & =-4.\end{aligned}
$$
